Weekly Sabbath
WEEK-lee SAB-bath
n. phrase
Weekly + Sabbath; distinguishing the seventh-day weekly Sabbath of the OT (and the Christian Lord’s Day under the New Covenant) from the various annual Sabbaths attached to feasts (e.g., the high Sabbath after Passover, the Sabbaths of the Day of Atonement and the Feast of Tabernacles).

📖 Biblical Definition

The weekly Sabbath is the recurring seventh-day Sabbath of Old Testament Israel, distinguished from the various annual Sabbaths attached to feasts (the high Sabbath after Passover; the Sabbaths of the Day of Atonement and the Feast of Tabernacles; the Sabbatical Year; the Year of Jubilee). The distinction is structurally important because, while the various annual and septennial Sabbaths were ceremonial-specific to the Mosaic economy and have been fulfilled and superseded in Christ (Col 2:16-17), the weekly Sabbath is grounded in creation itself—and God blessed the seventh day, and sanctified it: because that in it he had rested from all his work which God created and made (Gen 2:3)—and therefore stands as a creation ordinance distinct from the Mosaic ceremonial Sabbaths. The historic Reformed tradition has therefore made an important distinction: the Mosaic ceremonial Sabbaths (the annual feast-Sabbaths and the seventh-day specifically as Mosaic-ceremonial) are fulfilled in Christ and not binding on Christians; the weekly Sabbath-principle (one-day-in-seven set apart for worship and rest, grounded in creation and reaffirmed in the Decalogue’s grounding of the fourth commandment in the creation pattern) continues under the New Covenant, transposed to the Lord’s Day (first day of the week) commemorating the resurrection. The Lutheran and many Continental Reformed traditions have understood the matter somewhat differently, with less rigorous Sabbatarian application to the Lord’s Day; the Puritan-and-Presbyterian Reformed tradition has been more strict, treating the Lord’s Day with most of the weekly Sabbath’s discipline. The weekly Sabbath in the OT had several structural features. First, the cessation: ordinary work was to be suspended for the household, servants, foreigners, and even animals (Ex 20:10). Second, the worship: the Sabbath was a day of holy convocation (Lev 23:3), with the daily continual burnt offering doubled for the Sabbath (Num 28:9-10). Third, the redemption-remembrance: Deut 5:15 grounds the fourth commandment’s observance in the redemption from Egyptian slavery—the saint who rests on the Sabbath remembers that he was redeemed and therefore has a redeemed soul’s freedom to rest from labor. Fourth, the perpetual character: wherefore the children of Israel shall keep the sabbath, to observe the sabbath throughout their generations, for a perpetual covenant. It is a sign between me and the children of Israel for ever (Ex 31:16-17). The weekly Sabbath has therefore a creation-grounded substance that the New Covenant preserves under the Lord’s Day, with the specific day shifted and the ceremonial particulars of the Mosaic Sabbath fulfilled in Christ but the principle of one-day-in-seven worship-and-rest standing as a continuing creation-pattern for the people of God.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 distinguishes the weekly Sabbath (the seventh-day Sabbath grounded in creation) from the various annual Sabbaths of the Mosaic feasts; the former, by the historic Reformed tradition, continues under the New Covenant as the Christian Lord’s Day (first day of the week) commemorating the resurrection.

WEEKLY SABBATH — The seventh-day Sabbath of OT Israel, grounded in creation (Gen 2:3) and the fourth commandment (Ex 20:8-11), distinguished from the various annual Sabbaths attached to feasts. Under the New Covenant, the principle continues in the Christian Lord’s Day (first day of the week) commemorating the resurrection of Christ.

SEVENTH-DAY, a. — Pertaining to the seventh day of the week; the day of the weekly Sabbath in OT Israel.

📖 Key Scripture

Genesis 2:2-3 — "And on the seventh day God ended his work which he had made; and he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had made. And God blessed the seventh day, and sanctified it: because that in it he had rested from all his work which God created and made."

Exodus 20:8-11 — "Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy. Six days shalt thou labour, and do all thy work: But the seventh day is the sabbath of the LORD thy God: in it thou shalt not do any work... For in six days the LORD made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that in them is, and rested the seventh day: wherefore the LORD blessed the sabbath day, and hallowed it."

Exodus 31:16-17 — "Wherefore the children of Israel shall keep the sabbath, to observe the sabbath throughout their generations, for a perpetual covenant. It is a sign between me and the children of Israel for ever..."

Acts 20:7 — "And upon the first day of the week, when the disciples came together to break bread, Paul preached unto them, ready to depart on the morrow..."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The weekly Sabbath doctrine is corrupted, on one side, by the seventh-day-Adventist tradition that has insisted on continued seventh-day (Saturday) Sabbath observance for Christians, against the New Testament pattern of first-day gatherings—and on the other by the antinomian-grace tradition that has dropped the weekly Sabbath-principle entirely, treating any day-of-rest as legalistic bondage, against the creation-grounded pattern that predates Moses and continues under the new covenant in the Lord’s Day.

expand to see more

The seventh-day-Adventist tradition (and certain other Sabbatarian movements) has insisted on continued seventh-day (Saturday) Sabbath observance for Christians, on the grounds that the fourth commandment specifies the seventh day specifically and that the church’s shift to the first day was a post-apostolic Roman corruption. The historic orthodox tradition refuses this reading. The shift from the seventh day to the first is apostolic, attested in the NT (Acts 20:7, breaking bread on the first day; 1 Cor 16:2, collection on the first day; Rev 1:10, the Lord’s Day), and theologically grounded in the resurrection. The creation-grounded substance of the weekly Sabbath (one-day-in-seven worship-and-rest) continues; the specific day is shifted to honor the resurrection-event by which Christ’s redemptive work was sealed. The recovery is the recovery of the historic orthodox position: the weekly Sabbath-principle continues under the New Covenant in the Lord’s Day, with the specific day-of-the-week appropriately shifted to commemorate the resurrection.

The opposite corruption is the antinomian-grace tradition that has dropped the weekly Sabbath-principle entirely, treating any day-of-rest as legalistic bondage from which Christian liberty has freed the believer. This reading misses the creation-grounded substance of the principle. The weekly Sabbath is not chiefly a Mosaic ceremonial item that has been fulfilled in Christ (though the specifically Mosaic particulars have been); it is a creation ordinance grounded in the very pattern of God’s own work-and-rest, given to all humanity (not Israel only) at the creation, and reaffirmed in the Decalogue’s grounding of the fourth commandment in the creation pattern. To drop the weekly Sabbath-principle is to lose a creation-grounded pattern that predates Moses and continues under the new covenant. The Christian liberty Paul defends in Romans 14:5-6 and Col 2:16-17 is liberty over the specific particulars of OT Sabbath-observance, not abolition of the principle of weekly worship-and-rest. Recover both ends. Refuse the Sabbatarian insistence on the seventh day against the apostolic Lord’s Day, and refuse the antinomian abandonment of any weekly Sabbath-principle. The biblical pattern is the weekly Lord’s Day as the creation-grounded, Christ-centered, gospel-shaped day of worship and rest for the New Covenant people of God.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shabbāt (Sabbath) in its specifically weekly application; grounded in creation (Gen 2:3), codified in the Decalogue (Ex 20:8-11), distinguished from the Mosaic ceremonial annual Sabbaths; continues under the New Covenant in the Lord’s Day (first day of the week) commemorating the resurrection.

Hebrew shabbāt (H7676) — Sabbath (the weekly seventh-day rest).

Hebrew shibb’ī (H7637) — seventh (the ordinal number, of the seventh day).

Greek kuriakē hēmera — Lord’s Day (Rev 1:10).

Greek mia tōn sabbatōn — the first day of the week (Matt 28:1; Mark 16:2; Luke 24:1; John 20:1, 19; Acts 20:7; 1 Cor 16:2).
